Convert Sigma into an Effective Distance

Source: R/kernel_dist.R
kernel_dist.Rd

Converts a kernel scale parameter (sigma) into an effective distance in map units, the distance that holds a stated proportion of the kernel weight. Use it with a fitted multiScaleR object to report the estimated scales of effect as distances, or with kernel parameters you supply to explore how far a kernel reaches before fitting. The kernels, the two distance definitions, and their formulas are described in multiScaleR-kernels.

Usage

kernel_dist(model, prob = 0.9, dimension = c("2d", "1d"), ...)

Arguments

model

A fitted multiScaleR object from multiScale_optim(). When supplied, distances and 95% confidence limits are returned for every optimized covariate, and any sigma, kernel, or shape passed through ... is ignored with a warning. When omitted, supply sigma and kernel (and shape for "expow") through ....

prob

Numeric between 0 and 1 (exclusive). Proportion of the kernel weight that the reported distance must hold. Default: 0.9. Larger values give longer distances. Under dimension = "1d" the proportion is of the weight along a line through the point. Under "2d" it is of the weight on a plane.

dimension

Character. How the distance is measured. "2d" (default) returns the radius of the circle around the point that holds prob of the ideal kernel weight on an unbounded plane. "1d" returns the original line-based distance, which encloses prob of the area under the kernel curve along a transect through the point. For distance-weighted kernels the "2d" radius is longer than the "1d" distance. Hard-radius covariates in a fitted model report the same radius under both. See Details.

...

Kernel parameters used when model is not supplied:

  • sigma: positive numeric scalar. The kernel scale parameter, in the map units of the points and rasters passed to kernel_prep(). For the Gaussian kernel it is the standard deviation, for the negative exponential kernel the decay length, and for the fixed kernel the buffer radius.

  • kernel: character. One of "gaussian", "exp" (negative exponential), "expow" (exponential power), or "fixed" (fixed-radius buffer). Required.

  • shape: positive numeric scalar. Shape of the exponential power kernel. Required when kernel = "expow" and ignored otherwise.

  • beta: deprecated former name of shape. It is still accepted, with a warning, and will be removed in a future release. Supplying both shape and beta with different values is an error.

Value

When model is supplied, a data frame with one row per optimized covariate (row names are the covariate names) and three columns, all in map units and rounded to two decimal places:

  • Mean: the effective distance at the estimated sigma.

  • 2.5%: the distance at the lower 95% limit of sigma.

  • 97.5%: the distance at the upper 95% limit of sigma.

For a hard-radius covariate (a landscape metric, an unweighted surface metric, or any covariate fitted with kernel = "fixed"), the row reports the radius itself under either dimension. Limits are NA when no interval is available (see Details). A covariate whose sigma estimate is not finite returns NaN.

When kernel parameters are supplied through ..., a single numeric value, the distance in map units that holds prob of the kernel weight under the chosen dimension, rounded to two decimal places.

Read the distances

Sigma is a kernel parameter, not a radius. An effective distance puts the estimate in map units you can compare across kernels and studies. With sigma = 300 m, a Gaussian kernel holds 90% of its planar weight within about 644 m (dimension = "2d"), while the line-based 90% distance is about 493 m (dimension = "1d"). Use "2d" when you describe the area a kernel draws on, and always state the definition and the value of prob you report. The formulas for each kernel are tabulated in multiScaleR-kernels.

Both definitions describe the ideal continuous kernel. They do not account for truncation at max_D, raster edges, missing cells, or cell geometry, so the share of weight among the cells actually extracted around a point can differ. If the "2d" radius approaches or exceeds max_D, increase max_D in kernel_prep() and refit the model.

Reproduce distances from earlier versions

Versions 0.7.4 and later report dimension = "2d" distances by default in kernel_dist(), summary(), print(), and kernel plots. Earlier versions reported the line-based distance. The switch changes reporting only. It does not change fitted sigma values, kernel weights, or likelihoods. To reproduce distances reported by earlier versions, set the dimension explicitly:

kernel_dist(fit, dimension = "1d")
summary(fit, dimension = "1d")
print(fit, dimension = "1d")
plot(fit, dimension = "1d")
plot_kernel(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian", dimension = "1d")

Simulation extents in sim_dat(), the pct_wt window in kernel_scale.raster(), and the max_D warning of multiScale_optim() keep their line-based definitions.

Confidence limits from a fitted model

Each limit of sigma is converted to a distance with the same formula as the estimate. By default the sigma limits are Wald limits from the Hessian-based standard errors. When the fitted object stores its own interval table in profile_scale_est (see the fitted-object help page), those limits are used instead. summary(fit, profile = TRUE) converts profile-likelihood limits to distances in its own output, as described in summary.multiScaleR(). For exponential-power kernels, the shape is held at its estimate during this conversion, so the limits do not include uncertainty in the shape. These rules depend on the fitting route:

  • With backend = "profile_glm" or "joint_nb2" and an estimated exponential-power shape, distance limits use joint log-scale delta-method uncertainty for both sigma and shape. They remain Wald limits even when sigma limits are profiled in summary(), and they are missing when the fit fails the joint identifiability checks. Point distances remain available.

  • With backend = "conditional_logit", point distances are available but scale uncertainty has not been calibrated, so distance limits are missing.

  • With the default refit backend, point distances remain available when a sigma standard error is not finite, but its Wald limits are missing. When a smooth parameter sits at a search bound, the whole Wald block is withheld, while explicitly marked profile limits remain available.

  • A hard-radius covariate reports its radius directly and has no kernel shape, including in an exponential-power fit. It has no Hessian-based interval, but stored profile limits are kept. See the section on smooth kernels and hard radii in multiScaleR-kernels.

Native coefficient standard errors remain conditional on the selected scales. Manually supplied fixed-kernel parameters still return the requested weight quantile under the chosen dimension.

See also

multiScaleR-kernels for the kernel formulas and both distance definitions. summary.multiScaleR(), plot.multiScaleR(), and plot_kernel() report and draw the same distances. vignette("v02-user-guide", package = "multiScaleR") converts sigma to effective distances on a worked example.

Examples

## Distances from kernel parameters, without a fitted model
# A Gaussian kernel with sigma = 300 m: planar radius holding 90% of the weight
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian")                     # about 644
#> [1] 643.79
# The original line-based definition gives a shorter distance
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian", dimension = "1d")   # about 493
#> [1] 493.46
# Other kernels and proportions
kernel_dist(sigma = 500, kernel = "gaussian", prob = 0.95)
#> [1] 1223.87
kernel_dist(sigma = 100, kernel = "exp", prob = 0.975)
#> [1] 557.16
kernel_dist(sigma = 100, kernel = "expow", shape = 1.5, prob = 0.95)
#> [1] 235.51
kernel_dist(sigma = 100, kernel = "fixed")   # radius holding 90% of the buffer area
#> [1] 94.87

# \donttest{
## Distances from a fitted model
data("pts")
data("count_data")
hab <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "hab.tif",
                               package = "multiScaleR"))

kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts,
                             raster_stack = hab,
                             max_D = 250,
                             kernel = "gaussian",
                             verbose = FALSE)
mod <- glm(y ~ hab, family = poisson, data = count_data)
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod,
                        kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        verbose = FALSE)

# Planar radius (m) holding 90% of the weight, with limits from the
# 95% interval of sigma
kernel_dist(model = opt)
#>       Mean   2.5%  97.5%
#> hab 163.45 122.53 204.37
# Line-based distances, as reported before version 0.7.4
kernel_dist(model = opt, dimension = "1d")
#>       Mean  2.5%  97.5%
#> hab 125.28 93.92 156.65
# Radius holding 95% of the weight
kernel_dist(model = opt, prob = 0.95)
#>       Mean   2.5%  97.5%
#> hab 186.44 139.76 233.11
# }
